recent_posts.title: Tata and JSW to spend $1bn building India’s way out of Chinese battery dependence
recent_posts.summary: Tata Group and JSW Group are each funding separate R&D centres focused on next-generation battery chemistries and advanced EV systems, with a combined investment of nearly $1bn. The move is driven by India's heavy dependence on Chinese battery cells, materials, and equipment — a vulnerability that has become acute as Beijing tightens export controls on graphite, lithium-processing equipment, and battery-making machinery. Tata's effort is housed within Agratas, its battery arm already building a 20 GWh gigafactory in Gujarat, while JSW is operating through its JNEXT technology centre in Pune. Neither group expects to displace Chinese chemistry leadership this decade; the realistic goal is enough internal capability to specify, validate, and negotiate from a stronger position. The push mirrors Europe's battery sovereignty drive post-Northvolt, and complements India's existing PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells by finally adding private R&D capital to the equation.

recent_posts.title: Google updates AI Overviews with Further Exploration links, subscription labels as 58% publisher click decline triggers antitrust suits
recent_posts.summary: Google has announced five updates to AI Overviews and AI Mode aimed at driving more traffic to publishers: a Further Exploration links section, inline link context on desktop, subscription labels for news links, forum perspective previews, and expanded product review cards. The changes come amid a documented 58% decline in click-through rates correlated with AI Overviews, antitrust lawsuits from Penske Media, EU investigations under the Digital Markets Act, and a DOJ ruling against Google. Critics and publishers argue the updates are a tactical concession within a broader strategic shift toward AI-mediated search that structurally reduces the value of the open web, as Google simultaneously invests in agentic browsing and AI inference infrastructure that further reduces user incentive to visit publisher sites.

recent_posts.title: UFORCE, Ukraine's first defence tech unicorn, has conducted 150,000 combat missions as unmanned warfare goes commercial
recent_posts.summary: UFORCE, a Ukrainian-British defence tech startup formed from nine merged companies, has reached unicorn status with a $1B+ valuation after conducting over 150,000 combat missions since Russia's 2022 invasion. The company develops air, sea, and land drones — including MAGURA maritime drones that have struck 12 Russian warships — and is at the centre of what Ukraine claims was the first military operation in history where territory was seized using only unmanned systems. UFORCE employs 1,000+ engineers across six European countries, reported 450% booking growth in 2025, and raised $50M in March. The broader defence tech sector is booming, with European defence startups raising €2.3B in 2025. The shift toward autonomous weapons raises ethical questions around accountability and the delegation of lethal decisions to machines, while the UN has called for negotiations on autonomous weapons without producing a binding framework.

recent_posts.title: Ametek to buy Indicor's instrumentation businesses for $5bn
recent_posts.summary: Ametek has agreed to acquire the test-and-measurement businesses of Indicor for approximately $5bn, in what is the largest single partial exit Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has executed in 2026. CD&R originally acquired a 51% majority stake in Indicor — a 16-brand industrial instrumentation portfolio carved out of Roper Technologies in 2022 — at a $3.6bn enterprise value. The deal covers only the test-and-measurement subset; pumps-and-valves businesses remain with Indicor. The implied EBITDA multiple is 12–14x, putting CD&R on track for a 2.5–3.5x money multiple. Ametek's customer base spans semiconductor, pharma, aerospace, and energy sectors, positioning it as an indirect beneficiary of AI infrastructure buildout. The combined revenue base will approach $9bn. The deal is expected to close in H2 2026.

recent_posts.title: Davis raises $5.5m pre-seed to compress real-estate development
recent_posts.summary: Paris-based Davis has raised a $5.5m pre-seed co-led by Heartcore Capital and Balderton Capital to compress real-estate feasibility studies from months to days using AI. The company is launching Gaudi-1, a proprietary generative model that produces buildings as structured compositions of architectural elements rather than using diffusion-based image generation. Unlike typical PropTech SaaS, Davis sells finished feasibility studies and design concepts directly to real-estate developers, with human architects validating every output. The company claims state-of-the-art results on RPLAN and MSD benchmarks. Key risks include keeping the human validation layer efficient, handling regulatory complexity across jurisdictions, and competing with incumbents like Autodesk and Bentley.

recent_posts.title: Duolingo bets on engagement over monetization to outrun AI competition
recent_posts.summary: Duolingo beat Q1 2026 estimates with 27% revenue growth and 89 cents EPS, but its stock fell 14% after CEO Luis von Ahn announced a deliberate pivot away from near-term monetization toward engagement growth. The goal is to reach 100 million daily active users by 2028, nearly doubling the current 56.5 million. To get there, Duolingo is unlocking previously paywalled features, expanding AI-powered tutors like Video Call and Speaking Adventures, and leaning into gamification mechanics like streaks and leaderboards. The urgency stems from AI competition: ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and open-source models like Meta's Llama can now replicate language instruction at near-zero cost, threatening Duolingo's core curriculum moat. Von Ahn argues the real defensible asset is the daily habit loop, not the content itself. Investors are skeptical, with the stock now down over 40% in 2026 and roughly 80% from its all-time high.

recent_posts.title: The day after the $1.5bn JV, Anthropic shipped what the JV will sell
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4.7 and a suite of roughly ten pre-built AI agents targeting financial services workflows — pitchbooks, credit memos, KYC, AML investigations, and more. The release came one day after Anthropic announced a $1.5bn joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs. Key highlights include a Moody's native app covering 600 million companies embedded directly in Claude, an FIS-built Financial Crimes AI Agent going live at BMO and Amalgamated Bank to compress AML investigations from hours to minutes, and full Microsoft 365 integration. The agents run on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic's orchestration platform, shifting autonomous workflow execution to Anthropic's model layer rather than customer engineering teams. Risks flagged include regulatory scrutiny from the US Treasury, systemic concentration risk given Anthropic's growing role across major financial institutions, and competitive durability as OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft ship rival agent platforms.

recent_posts.title: Google, Microsoft, and xAI agree to pre-release government AI model evaluations as Mythos crisis forces oversight expansion
recent_posts.summary: Google, Microsoft, and xAI have joined OpenAI and Anthropic in voluntarily submitting AI models to the US Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation for pre-release evaluation. The expansion was catalysed by the 'Mythos crisis' — Anthropic's model capable of autonomously discovering zero-day vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers — which exposed the lack of formal government oversight for frontier AI. All five major frontier AI labs now participate, but the programme remains entirely voluntary with no statutory authority, no power to block releases, and fewer than 200 staff. Companies participate strategically to avoid mandatory legislation, while the Trump administration weighs an executive order that could formalise the process. The arrangement's core weakness is structural: it depends on goodwill, and any company could legally release a dangerous model without submitting it for review.

recent_posts.title: The $1.5m settlement that closes Musk's longest-running SEC matter
recent_posts.summary: Elon Musk has settled the SEC's four-year case over his late disclosure of a Twitter stake in 2022, agreeing to pay a $1.5m civil penalty with no admission of wrongdoing. The fine is the largest ever imposed by the SEC for a late Schedule 13D filing, yet represents less than 1% of the $150m harm the SEC alleged was caused to Twitter shareholders. Musk is not required to disgorge any gains from the allegedly under-priced share purchases. The SEC justified the settlement by arguing that further litigation would take years and that a settled penalty at the statutory maximum produces a more durable enforcement outcome. The resolution clears one of several open legal matters for Musk, as he faces ongoing proceedings including the OpenAI trial.

recent_posts.title: Apple wants a second source. Intel and Samsung want it to be them.
recent_posts.summary: Apple is in early-stage talks with Intel and Samsung to manufacture some of its M-series chips, marking a potential shift away from exclusive reliance on TSMC. The discussions are exploratory with no orders placed, and Apple has concerns about whether alternative foundries can match TSMC's yield and performance. The most likely scenario is using Intel or Samsung for lower-end M-series chips while keeping high-performance silicon on TSMC, with any non-TSMC shipments not expected until mid-2027. The move is driven by both geopolitical risk around Taiwan and commercial leverage, though yield gaps at both Intel Foundry and Samsung remain a significant challenge.
